2018 QCCS 3212

JK0261

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-17-091454-150

DATE:

July 23, 2018

BEFORE:

THE HONOURABLE

PETER KALICHMAN, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

JULES COHEN

Petitioner

v.

SUCCESSION DE FEU JOSEPH
COHEN

and

MTRE. AUDI GOZLAN

Defendants

And

SIMON
COHEN,

SALOMON
COHEN,

SCALI
HAIM COHEN,

and

MARC
MORDECHAI COHEN

Mis
en cause

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

(contestation of a will,
removal of a liquidator and damages)

______________________________________________________________________

OVERVIEW

[
1
]

The Plaintiff, Jules Cohen, is suing Mtre. Audi
Gozlan, the liquidator of the estate of his late brother, Joseph Cohen. He
seeks to have Joseph’s last will and testament set aside (the Will). In the
alternative, he asks the Court to declare invalid a legacy contained in the Will
and to relieve Mtre. Gozlan of his functions as liquidator.  Finally, he seeks
damages for defamation and for various slights that he claims to have suffered
as a result of the liquidator’s actions.

[
2
]

Jules
[1]
and the mis en cause Simon, Salomon, Scali and Marc, are the younger
brothers of Joseph.

[
3
]

On or about May 6, 2014, Joseph was admitted to
the Jewish General Hospital.  On May 12, 2014, while in the intensive care unit,
Joseph signed the Will.
[2]

[
4
]

The Will, prepared by Mtre. Gozlan, was
purportedly signed before two witnesses who are both colleagues of Mtre. Gozlan.
According to paragraph 4 of the Will, Joseph bequeaths his entire estate to
charitable causes in Israel but leaves it to his liquidator, Mtre. Gozlan, to
select which charities will benefit.

[
5
]

On or about June 9, 2014, Joseph was transferred
to the Jewish Eldercare Centre, a long-term facility adjacent to the hospital.
He remained there until his death on March 1, 2015.  Joseph was 83 years old.

[
6
]

Joseph’s funeral took place the next day.
Almost immediately following the funeral, Joseph’s body was transported to
Israel for burial in a plot that he had purchased years earlier.  Mtre. Gozlan
accompanied Joseph’s body and attended the burial that very evening in Israel.

[
7
]

On April 30, 2015, the Will was probated by Mtre.
Stéphanie Breton, Special Clerk.
[3]

[
8
]

Jules’ action raises the following questions:

(a)

Is the Will invalid
because the requirements of a will signed before witnesses were not met?

(b)

Is the universal legacy
created by paragraph 4 of the Will, valid?

(c)

If the universal
legacy is invalid and Joseph’s brothers become heirs to the estate, should Mtre.
Gozlan be removed as liquidator?

(d)

Is Jules entitled to
damages?

[
9
]

Before turning to the analysis, the Court will deal
with Jules’ request for a rendering of account.

[
10
]

In his action, Jules seeks an interim rendering
of account from Mtre. Gozlan. However, during the trial, Mtre. Gozlan
communicated an account. Neither party filed the account as evidence or
addressed it in closing arguments, possibly because Jules had not had the
opportunity to thoroughly review it. Under the circumstances, the Court will reserve
Jules’ right to claim that the account is not proper or complete and to ask for
the situation to be corrected, if need be.

ANALYSIS

(a)

Is the Will invalid because the
requirements of a will signed before witnesses were not met?

[
11
]

The rules pertaining to wills signed before
witnesses are contained in articles 727 and following of the
Civil Code of
Quebec
(CCQ).   To be valid, the will must be signed before two witnesses.  Art.
727 CCQ reads as follows:

727
. A will made in the presence of witnesses is
written by the testator or by a third person.

The testator then declares in the
presence of two witnesses of full age that the document he is presenting is his
will. He need not divulge its contents. He signs it at the end or, if he has
already signed it, acknowledges his signature; he may also cause a third person
to sign it for him in his presence and according to his instructions.

The witnesses sign the will forthwith
in the presence of the testator.

[
12
]

Jules submits that the Will is affected by two
irregularities that render it invalid.
[4]

The first irregularity pertains to the presence of the witnesses.  Jules claims
that Mtre. Barry Schrier, whose name appears on the Will as a witness, did not
in fact witness Joseph’s signature.  The second irregularity is the failure of
all parties to initial each page of the Will. The Court will examine each
alleged irregularity in turn.

[
13
]

With respect to the presence of Mtre. Schrier,
Jules’ position is based entirely on the testimony of Simon.  According to
Simon, who claims to have been by Joseph’s bedside during virtually his entire
stay in the hospital, Mtre. Gozlan was accompanied by a young woman when Joseph
signed the Will. However, Mtre. Schrier, who Simon had previously met on a
number of occasions, was not there.

[
14
]

Simon’s testimony is at odds not only with the
testimony of Mtre. Schrier but with that of Mtre. Gozlan and of Mtre. Zuker,
the second witness.  According to each of these witnesses, Mtre. Schrier
arrived after Mtre. Gozlan and Mtre. Zuker had already been with Joseph for
roughly 45 minutes, discussing the Will.  He stayed for approximately 10-15
minutes, witnessed Joseph’s signature and signed the Will himself.

[
15
]

The Court finds the testimony of the three
defence witnesses consistent and credible.  Consequently, Jules has failed to convince the Court on a balance of probabilities
that Mtre. Schrier did not witness Joseph’s signature on the Will.

[
16
]

With respect to the initialling of a will signed
before witnesses, Art. 728 CCQ reads as follows:

728
. Where
the will is written by a third person or by technical means, the testator and
the witnesses initial or sign each page of the act which does not bear their
signature.

The absence of initials or a signature
on each page does not prevent a will made before a notary that is not valid as
a notarial will from being valid as a will made in the presence of witnesses,
if the other formalities are observed.

[
17
]

It is clear that each page of the Will was not
initialled by Joseph and the two witnesses.  However, a will signed before
witnesses is not necessarily invalid simply because one of the formalities of
its execution is not respected. Art. 714 CCQ provides that such a will may
still be valid.

714
. A
holograph will or a will made in the presence of witnesses that does not fully Mtre.et
the requirements of that form is valid nevertheless if it meets the essential
requirements thereof and if it unquestionably and unequivocally contains the
last wishes of the deceased.

[
18
]

The requirement of initialling each page of a
will signed before witnesses is, therefore, not essential.
[5]
The Court must determine
whether the Will clearly and unequivocally contains the last wishes of Joseph.

[
19
]

Based primarily on the testimonial evidence of Mtre.
Gozlan and of Mtre. Zuker, the Court is satisfied that the Will reflects the
last wishes of Joseph. Joseph had been speaking to Mtre. Gozlan for years
regarding the terms of the Will. Mtre. Gozlan described in detail the evolution
of their discussions. In addition, Mtre. Gozlan continued to discuss the Will
with Joseph in the presence of Mtre. Zuker the day it was executed.

[
20
]

The Court adds that the principal purpose of initialling
the pages of a will signed before witnesses is to ensure that pages are not
added or altered after the fact. In this case, the Will is only three pages
long and its paragraphs are numbered consecutively. In short, it does not
appear that a page of the Will was added or removed.

(b)

Is the universal legacy created by
paragraph 4 of the Will, valid?

[
21
]

Paragraph 4 of the Will reads as follows:

Je désigne, donne et lègue à des
Oeuvres
de bienfaisance en Israël
tous mes biens mobiliers et immobiliers, réels et
personnels, de quelque nature qu’ils soient et a(sic) quelque emplacements
qu’ils soient, y compris les dépôts de banque, les liens de stocks, les
bénéfices des polices d’assurance, les projets d’économies de retraite
inscrits, et tout ce que je possède lors de ma mort, sans exception ni réserve.
Le choix des Oeuvres de bienfaisance est à la discrétion de l’Exécuteur testamentaire.

[
22
]

Jules submits that the legacy is invalid because
Joseph effectively delegated to his liquidator the power to name his beneficiaries.
He adds that such a delegation can only be valid if the testator transfers the
asset or assets into a separate and distinct patrimony, such as a trust.

[
23
]

Mtre. Gozlan submits that he and Joseph had numerous
discussions regarding the specific charitable organizations that should benefit
from Joseph’s legacy but never had the opportunity to finalize the list. He
adds that, in any event, the wording of paragraph six of the Will and,
specifically, the reference to seizin having been transferred to the liquidator,
indicates that a separate patrimony was created.

[
24
]

The Court agrees with Jules that the universal
legacy created in the fourth paragraph of the Will is invalid because it is
impossible to identify the legatees.

[
25
]

Similar to a legacy in favour of “government”
[6]
, “poor relations”
[7]
(
parents pauvres
), “charitable
causes”
[8]
,
“missionary purposes”
[9]
,
or for “assorted charities”
[10]

(charités diverses), each of which has been held to be invalid, Joseph’s legacy
is too vague and uncertain to be understood and applied.

[
26
]

Mtre. Gozlan indicates that he and Joseph had
discussed the choice of charities on numerous occasions and since Joseph gave
him the authority to make the final decision, his last wishes can still be
respected. The Court does not doubt that Joseph trusted Mtre. Gozlan but such a
delegation of authority is not valid.

[
27
]

Delegating the power to make a bequest amounts
to abdicating that power, which is contrary to the public order provision of
Art. 706 CCQ.
[11]

In essence, the power to designate a legatee belongs to the testator alone. It
is not for a third party or for the Court to make that decision for him.

[
28
]

That said, in the context of a trust, the settlor
can delegate to the trustee the power to appoint beneficiaries.
[12]
Such a delegation would be
possible in the context of a testamentary trust as well.
[13]
Does the Will create such
a trust?  The Court concludes that it does not.

[
29
]

The Will does not contain any of the formal
language found in the CCQ for the creation of a trust.  However, as Justice
Kasirer noted in the Court of Appeal’s decision in
Groupe Sutton-Royal inc.
(Syndic de)
: “As long as the requirements for the establishment of a trust
set forth in articles 1260 et seq. C.C.Q. are satisfied, the fact that the
parties did not use express terminology of the trust in their dealings is not,
in itself, an impediment to the constitution of a trust.”
[14]
The key consideration is
whether or not the settlor’s intention to create a trust is established by the
evidence.

[
30
]

In the present case, not only are the essential
requirements not satisfied, but the evidence suggests that it was not Joseph’s
intention to create a trust.

[
31
]

One of the three essential conditions for the
establishment of a trust is that the settlor must transfer property from his
patrimony to another patrimony, which is autonomous and distinct from that of
the settlor.
[15]

Nothing in the Will suggests even implicitly, that such a separate patrimony
was constituted.

[
32
]

With respect to Joseph’s intentions, Mtre.
Gozlan indicates that they had discussed possible charities but did not have
the chance to finalize the selection.  The idea that Joseph was to finalize the
selection himself is inconsistent with the suggestion that it was his intention
to create a trust and delegate to Mtre. Gozlan the discretion to choose the
beneficiaries.  The Court concludes that it was not Joseph’s intention to
create a trust.

[
33
]

The universal legacy created in paragraph 4 of
the Will is therefore invalid.

(c)

If the universal legacy is invalid and
Joseph’s brothers become heirs to the estate, should Mtre. Gozlan be removed as
liquidator?

[
34
]

Having determined that the universal legacy set
out in the fourth paragraph of the Will is invalid, the property left by Joseph
remains in his intestate succession.
[16]

Jules and his brothers are therefore heirs to Joseph’s estate.

[
35
]

Jules argues that given the obvious conflict
that exists between Mtre. Gozlan and Joseph’s surviving brothers, Mtre. Gozlan
should be replaced as the liquidator.

[
36
]

Mtre. Gozlan opposes his removal as liquidator.
He would like to finish the job that Joseph selected him for and adds that it
would be inefficient and wasteful for another liquidator to take over at this
point.

[
37
]

The Court agrees with Mtre. Gozlan that he
should remain as liquidator. Jules has failed to convince the Court that the
magnitude of the conflict between Mtre. Gozlan and Joseph’s surviving brothers
justifies the Court taking the extreme step of removing a liquidator who was
specifically appointed by the testator.
[17]

[
38
]

The liquidator to an estate can be removed when
he is unable to assume his responsibilities, when he neglects his duties or
when he fails to fulfill his obligations.
[18]

The Court finds no evidence of any such failure.

[
39
]

In the present case, the replacement is
requested on the basis of personal animosity that Jules expects will make it
impossible for him and his brothers to work with Mtre. Gozlan in order to
finalize the estate.  From their testimony, it is clear that Joseph’s brothers
resent Mtre. Gozlan’s involvement in their brother’s life and in the administration
of his estate.   However, the replacement of a liquidator is not an appropriate
remedy in order to resolve or avoid a dispute with the heirs over the manner in
which the liquidator should proceed.
[19]

The conflict that Jules anticipates has not had an impact on the administration
of the estate and, if the parties conduct themselves with mutual respect, it
should not have such an impact.

(d)

Is Jules entitled to damages?

[
40
]

Jules claims $15,000.00 in damages from Mtre.
Gozlan.  His allegations of fault center around two main issues.

[
41
]

First, Jules claims that Mtre. Gozlan cut him
and his brothers out of Joseph’s life in his final months and effectively
prevented them from fulfilling their duty of making his funeral and burial
arrangements.   He claims that Joseph’s funeral was supposed to have been at
Papermans, which the parties agree is a well-known and prestigious funeral home.
As well, Joseph’s body should have been accompanied by one of his brothers on
the trip to Israel and not by Mtre. Gozlan.

[
42
]

Second, Jules claims that Mtre. Gozlan
humiliated him and his family by spreading rumours that Joseph died penniless.
He refers in particular to a Facebook message posted by Mtre. Gozlan’s wife in
which she solicits funds to pay for Mtre. Gozlan’s trip to Israel to accompany
Joseph’s body.

[
43
]

For the reasons that follow, the Court finds
that Jules’ damage claim is without merit.

[
44
]

There is no evidence that Mtre. Gozlan excluded
Jules or his brothers from any aspect of Joseph’s life or the preparations for
his funeral or burial.  Mtre. Gozlan’s involvement was in accordance with
Joseph’s wishes as expressed, primarily, in the Will.  As far as the choice of
funeral home is concerned, there is no evidence that Joseph had left specific
instructions in this regard or that funds were available for a burial at
Papermans, which is considerably more expensive than the funeral home that Mtre.
Gozlan selected.
[20]

[
45
]

It is clear that Jules was not very involved in
Joseph’s life in the months before his death. In fact, Jules did not see Joseph
from the time he left the hospital in June 2014 until his death in March 2015. There
appears to have been a rift of some sort between them.  Although Joseph blames this
rift on Mtre. Gozlan, the Court finds no evidence to support this assertion.
[21]

[
46
]

In regards to the burial, it appears that at some
point it had been agreed between the brothers that Simon would accompany
Joseph’s body to Israel for burial.  However, Simon was ill when Joseph died
and could not make the trip.  Jules indicates that he had obligations that
prevented him from going but that one of his other brothers could have made the
trip had Mtre. Gozlan not taken that decision out of their hands.

[
47
]

Contrary to Jules’ testimony, however, none of
his other brothers were able or willing to accompany Joseph’s body to Israel.
At the funeral, Mtre. Gozlan requested of Jules and his brothers that they
assist him in paying for the costs associated with the trip to Israel.
[22]
At the time, not one of
them indicated he would go in place of Mtre. Gozlan or that Mtre. Gozlan should
not go.

[
48
]

The Court concludes that Mtre. Gozlan’s decision
to accompany Joseph’s body to Israel was motivated by respect for Joseph,
respect for the traditions associated with Orthodox Judaism, a sense of duty to
a client and friendship.  There is no suggestion that Mtre. Gozlan in any way
profited from the trip. In fact, it appears that all or at least part of the
trip was at his own expense in addition to the cost associated with leaving his
law practice on short notice for several days.

[
49
]

With respect to the claim of humiliation, Jules
has failed to convince the Court that Mtre. Gozlan made any statements that
disparaged Joseph or dishonoured his memory.   On the contrary, the Court finds
that Mtre. Gozlan treated Joseph with respect that extended beyond the
boundaries of their professional relationship.

[
50
]

The Facebook post written by Mtre. Gozlan’s
wife, which Jules claims is defamatory, gives an indication of the nature of
the relationship between Joseph and Mtre. Gozlan’s family.  While it contains a
request to a select group of friends for financial assistance in regards to Mtre.
Gozlan’s trip to Israel, the Court finds nothing disrespectful much less
defamatory in the text, which reads as follows:

Today we lost someone very dear to
us. Joseph it was such a privilege to know u. To help u. To laugh with u and to
receive ur blessings. We will miss u dearly. U have ur plot in Israel waiting
for u. Audi will bring u. We do need help. Anything u can give will help tremendously.
Pm me if u can give especially a few days before purim. Thank u.
[23]

[
51
]

Even though Jules’ claim for damages is
dismissed, the Court is not without sympathy for the emotional toll that
Joseph’s death has taken not only on Jules but on his family.  It is clear that
Joseph played a pivotal role in the history of the Cohen family, who lost their
father at an early age.  Jules, Simon, Scali and Solomon all speak of their
older brother with reverence, respect and love. The text of Jules’ eulogy
illustrates the depth of his affection for Joseph.
[24]

[
52
]

The Court does not doubt that Jules would have
wanted to be more involved in the funeral and burial arrangements for Joseph
and senses his frustration and sadness over the manner in which the decisions
regarding these important rituals were taken. However, it was Joseph, who was
clearly strong-willed and independent, who placed his trust in Mtre. Gozlan and
involved him in his affairs.  There is no evidence that Mtre. Gozlan
manipulated Joseph or in any way took advantage of him.

[
53
]

While communications between Mtre. Gozlan and
Joseph’s surviving brothers have at times been difficult and strained, they all
clearly share a great affection and respect for Joseph. The Court hopes that
this common thread will allow them to finalize the details of Joseph’s estate
in a manner that befits his memory.

[
54
]

Finally, given the nature of the dispute and the
mitigated result, the Court awards no costs.

FOR THESE
REASONS, THE COURT:

MAINTAINS
in part Petitioner’s Demand;

DECLARES
invalid the universal legacy contained in the fourth paragraph of
the last will and testament of Joseph Cohen dated May 12, 2014;

RESERVES
Petitioner’s rights in regards to an interim rendering of account
by the liquidator;

WITHOUT
legal costs.

PETER KALICHMAN, J.S.C.
